\chapter{Ir in the Plural --- a Verb That Is Not Ir}
\label{ch:spanish-ir-plural}
\hlchaptermodality{57}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use ir in every person, and say why its present belongs to a different verb.}

The present of ir is regular for vadere - and the four commonest verbs are now complete.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vamos · vais]{vamos — from a verb that is not \emph{ir}}

\label{lesson:ES-C10-vamos}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I go.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Voy}.) And \textquotedblleft{}we speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablamos}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -amos and -áis, on a stem you have not seen}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{vamos} — \emph{we go.}  ·  \textbf{vais} — \emph{you all go.}
\end{quote}

The endings are ordinary. \textbf{-amos} and \textbf{-áis} are the plain \emph{-ar} endings from \emph{hablamos} and \emph{habláis}.

What is strange is the stem. The infinitive is \emph{ir}, and there is no \emph{v} in it anywhere — yet every one of these forms begins with one.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
You met this shape two chapters ago and now you can use it as a tool.

\textbf{Ir is not one verb.} Latin had \textbf{īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}, which gives the infinitive \emph{ir} and little else. It also had \textbf{vādere}, \textquotedblleft{}to advance, to make one's way\textquotedblright{}, which gives \emph{voy}, \emph{vas}, \emph{va}, \emph{vamos}, \emph{vais} and one more — the entire present tense.

So the present of \emph{ir} is not irregular. It is \textbf{regular for a different verb}, one whose infinitive Spanish stopped using. The endings behave perfectly; they are simply attached to a stem the dictionary form does not show you.

That is the third time this pattern has explained something: \emph{ser} from \emph{esse} and \emph{sedēre}, and now \emph{ir} from \emph{īre} and \emph{vādere}. \textbf{English does it too} — \emph{go} and \emph{went}, where \emph{went} is really the past of \emph{wend}.

\begin{quote}
The commonest verbs in a language are the likeliest to be made of more than one, because they are used so much that no single word's forms survive intact.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablamos, vamos\textquotedblright{} — the same ending, an unexpected stem
  \item \textquotedblleft{}voy, vas, va, vamos, vais\textquotedblright{} — all one verb, and it is not \emph{ir}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}we go\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Vamos}.) Which Latin verb do these forms come from? (\emph{\textbf{Vādere}}.) And what does that make \emph{ir}? (\textbf{Two verbs}, like \emph{ser} — and like English \emph{go} and \emph{went}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[van]{van — and the four are done}

\label{lesson:ES-C10-van}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}we go.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Vamos}.) And \textquotedblleft{}they speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablan}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the last form}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{van} — \emph{they go}, and \textbf{ustedes van}, \emph{you all go}.
\end{quote}

Latin's form was \emph{vadunt}. Spanish wore it down to three letters, and the rule still holds visibly: a final \textbf{-n}, and the subject is plural and not you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four chapters ago you could conjugate any \emph{regular} verb in the present, and none of the irregular ones. Now the four commonest verbs in Spanish are complete in every person:

\textbf{ser} · \textbf{estar} · \textbf{tener} · \textbf{ir} — \emph{to be}, \emph{to be}, \emph{to have}, \emph{to go}.

And each one taught something that outlives it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\textbf{ser}} — two Latin verbs fused, so the seam shows at \emph{eres}.
  \item \emph{\textbf{estar}} — one verb, so it is regular; the accent only marks stress.
  \item \emph{\textbf{tener}} — the stem breaks exactly where it is stressed, in \textbf{every} stem-changing verb, which is why \emph{nosotros} and \emph{vosotros} never break.
  \item \emph{\textbf{ir}} — its present belongs to a different verb entirely.
\end{itemize}

Three of those four are about the same underlying thing: \textbf{a verb that looks chaotic is usually more than one word}, and the places it looks regular are the places one word survived intact.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}somos, estamos, tenemos, vamos\textquotedblright{} — the four, in the \emph{we} form
  \item \textquotedblleft{}son, están, tienen, van\textquotedblright{} — the four, in the \emph{they} form
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until all four run without a gap.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}they go\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Van}.) Name the four verbs you have just completed. (\emph{Ser, estar, tener, ir}.) And what do three of them have in common? (Each is \textbf{more than one Latin verb}, or its stem change follows the stress.)
\end{tcolorbox}
